title: Three ordinal-indexed comparisons of products with iterated Z hold at every countable ordinal
source_title: Scott sentence complexities of linear orderings

standard_prerequisites.name: Iterated products with Z
standard_prerequisites.statement: Z^alpha is the alpha-fold lexicographic product of the integers with itself, and Z^alpha times L is the product of that order with L.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the orders the three families of statements compare.

standard_prerequisites.name: Back-and-forth relations and their rank shift
standard_prerequisites.statement: The rank two alpha, two alpha plus one and two alpha plus two relations are decided by intervals of the products, whose form fixes how many moves the comparison costs.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the relations the three statements assert at those ranks.

standard_prerequisites.name: Initial and final segments of the products
standard_prerequisites.statement: An initial segment of Z^alpha times L above a chosen point is again a product with an infinite order, and the same holds for final segments.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the orders appearing in the interval cases the proof checks.

core_obligations: State the three families A_alpha, B_alpha and C_alpha and note that A_0 and B_0 are trivial, so the induction only needs the successor and limit steps (source lines 1160-1162).

From B_alpha derive A_{alpha+1}: choose a tuple in the product and build a matching tuple by keeping points inside the same copy or jumping two copies ahead, then verify the three interval cases that remain, each of which is an instance of B_alpha (source lines 1163-1188).
From B_alpha derive C_alpha: place the matching tuple inside the initial Z^alpha times omega and check the two interval cases left over, again by B_alpha (source lines 1190-1207).

From C_alpha and A_{alpha+1} derive B_{alpha+1}: match the finitely many copies of Z^{alpha+1} using the cardinality hypothesis and preserve successor and endpoint positions, then check the five interval cases, three by A_{alpha+1} and the remaining two by reducing to C_alpha (source lines 1209-1237).

Close the limit step: A_lambda follows from the A_gamma below it, and B_lambda follows from A_lambda together with the C_gamma below it, after the same reduction to a single interval case (source lines 1239-1264).

proof_roadmap.step: Set up the three families and their trivial base cases.
B_alpha implies A_{alpha+1} through the three interval cases.
B_alpha implies C_alpha through the two interval cases.
C_alpha and A_{alpha+1} imply B_{alpha+1} through five cases.
Limit levels, where the same reduction is made once more.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled lemma at source0.tex lines 1147-1158: three families of statements indexed by a countable ordinal, comparing products of the form Z^alpha times an order at ranks two alpha, two alpha plus one and two alpha plus two under a cardinality hypothesis and an absence of last elements respectively, hold at every countable ordinal. The statement gives no hint of the induction structure, and the proof (source lines 1160-1266) is a mutual transfinite induction in which each successor step has to be pushed through explicit back-and-forth bookkeeping: the tuple chosen by the opponent is matched copy by copy, the intervals that remain are classified into three, two and five cases respectively, and each case is then discharged by one of the other families; the limit step needs the same classification once more, with the last case reduced to the C family below the limit. The cardinality hypothesis is used to match copies and to preserve successor and endpoint positions, and nothing of this machinery is visible in the statement.
